source_metadata.title: Authoring and Management of Transparent Research Integrity Assessments of Randomised Clinical Trial Publications Using LLM-assisted Tools and Provenance Knowledge Graphs
source_metadata.source_type: arXiv preprint; AI-assisted research-integrity tooling, ontology, and knowledge-graph evaluation paper

extraction_metadata.scope: Main-text independently reviewable assertions; bibliography entries were treated as provenance infrastructure rather than extraction targets.

atoms.canonical_statement: The work presents INSPECT-AI, RIPE-O, and RIPE-KG as an end-to-end pipeline for performing, documenting, and publishing provenance-rich research integrity assessments of randomized controlled trial publications.
The project used agile, iterative, end-to-end software prototyping to support interdisciplinary knowledge transfer and refine requirements with biomedical and technical team members.
The team chose a human-in-the-loop design rather than a fully automated AI application after iterative prototyping exposed practical limitations of AI in the assessment context.
Biomedical researchers provided 50 diverse real-world problematic publications and detailed assessment guidance to mitigate domain-knowledge gaps among computer scientists.
Provenance graphs were generated from INSPECT-AI process logs using YARRRML mappings.
RIPE-O was developed using the four-stage Linked Open Terms methodology, with competency questions guided by selected INSPECT-SR checks and framed by the 7Ws of provenance.
RIPE-O extends TIDO, which aligns with PROV-O, and reuses SPAR ontologies including FABIO and CITO for bibliographic modeling.
The RIPE-O ontology was checked with the OntOlogy Pitfall Scanner and validated by translating competency questions into SPARQL queries and testing them against real-world INSPECT-AI evaluation data.
INSPECT-AI uses GROBID to extract publication metadata including DOI, title, authors, and references from uploaded PDFs.
INSPECT-AI uses Gemini 2.0 Flash to extract registration identifiers and study-timeline information from publication text, with a short rationale attached to each extracted evidence item.
LLM-generated evidence is treated as a suggestion that reviewers can correct or override before the final integrity assessment is recorded.
INSPECT-AI queries Retraction Watch and PubPeer using extracted publication metadata and queries ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP when trial registration identifiers are available.
Collected evidence is evaluated against individual INSPECT-SR checks using predefined conditional rules that generate suggested outcomes such as concerns found or unclear evidence.

For prospective registration, INSPECT-AI compares the recruitment start date with the registration date and suggests retrospective-registration concerns when registration occurred after recruitment began.
The INSPECT-AI interface presents the publication, collected evidence, and suggested outcomes to a reviewer who can accept, modify, or override the suggestion and record a rationale.
Evidence items, assessment data, and participating agents are logged as provenance information in a PostgreSQL database.
The INSPECT-AI pilot included 13 volunteers from the University of Aberdeen, University of Manchester, and Indiana University during October-November 2025.
Pilot participants used INSPECT-AI to assess 69 publications.

RIPE-O models research-integrity assessment provenance using PROV-style activities, entities, and agents, linking evidence aggregation, evaluation activities, questions, hypotheses, and human or automated assessors.
RIPE-O is intended to be generic: it does not prescribe which integrity questions must be investigated and can represent new questions beyond the initial INSPECT-SR checks.
RIPE-KG is accessible through a SPARQL endpoint and a web-based graphical interface.
At the time of writing, RIPE-KG contained 140 research-integrity assessments.

atoms.canonical_statement: The current INSPECT-AI prototype does not provide AI support for all INSPECT-SR checks.
RIPE-KG inherits limitations from OpenAlex because author disambiguation depends on OpenAlex metadata.
INSPECT-AI functionality depends on the quality and completeness of external sources including SemOpenAlex, Retraction Watch, and PubPeer.

The authors describe the work as the first end-to-end pipeline for generating provenance traces of research-integrity assessments and publishing them as open knowledge graphs aligned with FAIR principles.
The authors argue that observed discrepancies support retaining human validation in LLM-based decision-support systems for research-integrity assessment.

Planned work includes extending INSPECT-SR check coverage, applying RIPE-O beyond the initial biomedical setting, expanding RIPE-KG through trusted users, and exploring graph-based selection of potentially untrustworthy publications for human assessment.
The work was supported by the Economic and Social Research Council under grant UKRI1083, with additional acknowledged support for the University of Aberdeen Interdisciplinary Institute.
The authors report using generative AI for LaTeX formatting, text-shortening suggestions, and programming support including query and code generation for INSPECT-AI and the RIPE-KG web interface.
The paper provides permanent w3id identifiers for the RIPE Observatory, INSPECT-AI, RIPE-O, and RIPE-KG, and cites public GitHub documentation for LLM prompts and mappings.

extraction_limitations: This source is a software/ontology/knowledge-graph research paper rather than a clinical primary-study report; the current LiteratureAtom schema is oriented toward primary literature, so software-system exposures and evaluation populations are represented with the closest available generic fields.

The source reports a feasibility/usability pilot without inferential statistics, confidence intervals, or a prespecified comparative control; quantitative atoms therefore preserve descriptive counts and percentages only.
No conflict-of-interest statement or standalone conventional data-availability statement was identified in the main text; no such content was invented.
References were inspected for source context but were not atomized as independent evidence claims.
